defects-diffusion-001.question: Among point defects in ionic crystals, which correctly describes a Frenkel defect?
choices: A pair consisting of a cation vacancy and an anion vacancy
A pair consisting of a vacancy and an interstitial ion, formed when an ion leaves its lattice site and moves into an interstitial position
An ion of an element different from the host substituting on a lattice site
defects-diffusion-001.explanation: A Frenkel defect forms when an ion (usually the smaller cation) moves from its lattice site to an interstitial position, creating a vacancy and an interstitial ion as a pair. Ag⁺ in AgCl and AgBr is the well-known example. A pair of a cation vacancy and an anion vacancy is a Schottky defect, which occurs mainly in NaCl and MgO. Both combinations preserve the electrical neutrality of the crystal as a whole. Substitution by a foreign ion is impurity solid solution; when the valences differ, vacancies or other defects are introduced to compensate the charge.

defects-diffusion-002.question: Which correctly describes the relation between the Burgers vector and the dislocation line of an edge dislocation?
choices: They are perpendicular to each other
They are parallel to each other
They always make an angle of 45°
defects-diffusion-002.explanation: An edge dislocation has the form of an extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the crystal, and its Burgers vector b is perpendicular to the dislocation line. An edge dislocation glides in the direction of b, and its slip plane is uniquely defined as the plane containing both b and the line. b is parallel to the line in a screw dislocation; because a screw dislocation has no unique slip plane, it can cross-slip onto another slip plane. Most real dislocations are mixed dislocations in between, with the proportions of edge and screw character changing continuously along the line, so there is no fixed 45°.

defects-diffusion-003.question: A metal has a vacancy formation energy of 0.90 eV. Using n/N = exp(−Q/kT), which value is closest to the equilibrium vacancy concentration (the fraction of lattice sites that are vacant) at 1000 K? Take Boltzmann's constant as k = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K.
defects-diffusion-003.explanation: kT = 8.617×10⁻⁵ × 1000 ≈ 0.0862 eV, so Q/kT = 0.90/0.0862 ≈ 10.44. Then n/N = exp(−10.44) ≈ 2.9×10⁻⁵, or one vacancy for roughly every 35,000 lattice sites. About 5.4×10⁻³ is the mistake of halving the exponent to exp(−Q/2kT), confusing it with the expression for the carrier density of an intrinsic semiconductor. About 3.6×10⁻¹¹ is the mistake of computing 10 to the power −10.44 with a common logarithm instead of exp. The vacancy concentration rises exponentially with temperature and reaches around 10⁻⁴ near the melting point.

defects-diffusion-004.question: Carbon diffuses at steady state through a 5.0 mm thick steel plate whose two faces are held at carbon concentrations of 1.2 kg/m³ and 0.8 kg/m³. If the diffusion coefficient is 3.0×10⁻¹¹ m²/s, which value is closest to the diffusion flux of carbon? Assume the concentration varies linearly through the thickness.
defects-diffusion-004.explanation: At steady state, Fick's first law J = −D(dC/dx) applies. The concentration gradient is (0.8 − 1.2)/(5.0×10⁻³ m) = −80 kg/m⁴, so J = 3.0×10⁻¹¹ × 80 = 2.4×10⁻⁹ kg/(m²·s), flowing from the high-concentration side to the low-concentration side. About 2.4×10⁻¹² is a unit-conversion error from dividing by the thickness left as 5.0 in mm, and about 7.2×10⁻⁹ uses the concentration on one side, 1.2 kg/m³, instead of the concentration difference. It is the concentration difference that drives the flow, so getting the gradient right matters. The same approach is used in hydrogen permeation tests and in evaluating gas separation membranes.

defects-diffusion-005.question: The diffusion coefficient of carbon in γ-iron follows the Arrhenius form D = D₀exp(−Q/RT) with D₀ = 2.3×10⁻⁵ m²/s and activation energy Q = 148 kJ/mol. Which value is closest to the diffusion coefficient at 927 °C? Take the gas constant as R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
defects-diffusion-005.explanation: Convert the temperature to absolute temperature: T = 927 + 273 = 1200 K. Q/RT = 148000/(8.314 × 1200) ≈ 14.83, so D = 2.3×10⁻⁵ × exp(−14.83) ≈ 2.3×10⁻⁵ × 3.6×10⁻⁷ ≈ 8.3×10⁻¹² m²/s. About 1.1×10⁻¹³ is the mistake of substituting the temperature as 927 in °C. About 2.3×10⁻⁵ is the mistake of leaving Q as 148 in kJ, which makes the exponent nearly zero and gives almost the same value as D₀. Because D changes exponentially with temperature, raising the carburizing temperature by just a few tens of degrees can shorten the treatment time considerably.

defects-diffusion-006.question: The diffusion coefficient of an element was 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ m²/s at 800 K and 4.0×10⁻¹³ m²/s at 1000 K. Assuming the Arrhenius form D = D₀exp(−Q/RT), which value is closest to the activation energy Q? Take R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
defects-diffusion-006.explanation: Taking the ratio of the expressions at the two temperatures eliminates D₀ and gives ln(D₂/D₁) = (Q/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂). D₂/D₁ = 40, ln 40 ≈ 3.689 and 1/800 − 1/1000 = 2.5×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, so Q = 8.314 × 3.689 / (2.5×10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.23×10⁵ J/mol, about 123 kJ/mol. About 53 kJ/mol uses the common logarithm (log₁₀ 40 ≈ 1.602) instead of the natural logarithm, and about 245 kJ/mol is double the value, from confusing the expression with the form exp(−Q/2RT). In practice, ln D is plotted against 1/T and Q is obtained from the slope −Q/R of the straight line.

defects-diffusion-007.question: A steel containing 0.20 wt% carbon is carburized with its surface carbon concentration held at 1.00 wt%. Which value is closest to the time needed for the carbon concentration to reach 0.60 wt% at a depth of 0.50 mm? Take the diffusion coefficient as 1.6×10⁻¹¹ m²/s, (C − C₀)/(Cₛ − C₀) = 1 − erf(x/2√(Dt)), erf(0.371) = 0.40 and erf(0.477) = 0.50.
defects-diffusion-007.explanation: (0.60 − 0.20)/(1.00 − 0.20) = 0.50, so 1 − erf(z) = 0.50 and erf(z) = 0.50 give z = x/2√(Dt) = 0.477. Then √(Dt) = 0.50×10⁻³/(2 × 0.477) ≈ 5.24×10⁻⁴ m, Dt ≈ 2.75×10⁻⁷ m², and t = 2.75×10⁻⁷/(1.6×10⁻¹¹) ≈ 1.72×10⁴ s, about 4.8 hours. About 19 hours is the mistake of dropping the 2 in the denominator and setting x/√(Dt) = 0.477, which makes the time four times too long. About 7.9 hours ignores the initial carbon concentration C₀ and uses 0.60/1.00, giving erf(z) = 0.40 and z = 0.371. Because the time is proportional to the square of the depth, how the factors are handled has a large effect.

defects-diffusion-008.question: In a diffusion treatment at a fixed temperature, by what factor must the treatment time be increased to double the depth at which a given concentration is reached?
defects-diffusion-008.explanation: In the error-function solution the concentration depends only on x/2√(Dt), so the depth x at which a given concentration is reached is proportional to √(Dt). At the same temperature D is constant, so doubling the depth requires doubling √t, that is, four times the time. Two times assumes the depth is proportional to time, and √2 times applies the proportionality the wrong way round. The diffusion-distance estimate x ≈ √(Dt) is used in many situations, including carburizing and dopant diffusion. When a deep layer is needed, raising the temperature to increase D is more effective than extending the time.

defects-diffusion-009.question: In α-iron at the same temperature, the diffusion coefficient of carbon is many orders of magnitude larger than that of nickel. Which is the main reason?
choices: Carbon moves between interstitial sites, so it can jump even without a neighboring vacancy
Carbon diffuses by the vacancy mechanism, and vacancies tend to gather around carbon atoms
Carbon has a smaller atomic mass than nickel, so its thermal vibrations are faster
defects-diffusion-009.explanation: Small atoms such as carbon sit in the gaps between iron atoms (interstitial sites) and can jump one after another into neighboring empty interstitial sites. Since almost all interstitial sites are empty, jump opportunities are plentiful and the activation energy is small. Substitutional atoms such as nickel diffuse by the vacancy mechanism and can move only when a vacancy arrives next to them; the vacancy formation energy is added to the activation energy, making diffusion far slower. The difference in vibration frequency due to atomic mass plays a minor role, but only the difference in diffusion mechanism can explain a gap of many orders of magnitude.

defects-diffusion-010.question: Which statement about diffusion paths in a polycrystalline metal is correct?
choices: The activation energy generally increases in the order lattice diffusion < grain boundary diffusion < surface diffusion
The lower the temperature, the larger the contribution of grain boundary diffusion relative to lattice diffusion
The finer the grains, the smaller the contribution of grain boundary diffusion
defects-diffusion-010.explanation: The more disordered the atomic packing along a path, the more easily atoms jump, so the activation energy generally increases in the order surface diffusion < grain boundary diffusion < lattice (volume) diffusion. The first choice has this order reversed. Paths with lower activation energy lose less of their diffusion coefficient as the temperature falls, so the relative contribution of grain boundary diffusion grows at lower temperatures. Finer grains mean a larger total grain boundary area, so the contribution of grain boundary diffusion actually increases. This is why grain boundary diffusion becomes a problem in low-temperature, fine-grained systems such as solder joints and thin-film interconnects.

defects-diffusion-011.question: When copper and brass (a Cu-Zn alloy) are bonded and heated, inert markers placed at the original interface move toward the brass side (the Kirkendall effect). What does this phenomenon show?
choices: The two kinds of atoms diffuse at different rates, and substitutional diffusion is occurring by exchange with vacancies
Atoms diffuse only by the interstitial mechanism, and the number of lattice sites does not change
The markers are being pushed along by thermal stress generated at the interface
defects-diffusion-011.explanation: Zinc diffuses into copper faster than copper diffuses into brass, so more atoms leave the brass side than enter it. Substitutional diffusion proceeds by exchange with vacancies, so vacancies flow opposite to the net flow of atoms; lattice planes are lost on the brass side and the markers shift toward the brass. This historic experiment showed that diffusion proceeds by the vacancy mechanism. With only the interstitial mechanism, the number of lattice sites would not change and the markers would not move. Excess vacancies that coalesce form Kirkendall voids, which degrade the reliability of solder joints and similar structures.

defects-diffusion-012.question: The Burgers vector of a perfect dislocation in an FCC metal is (a/2)<110>. Which value is closest to its magnitude in aluminum (lattice parameter 0.405 nm)?
defects-diffusion-012.explanation: The magnitude of (a/2)<110> is (a/2) × √(1² + 1² + 0²) = a/√2, so 0.405/1.414 ≈ 0.286 nm. This equals the nearest-neighbor distance in FCC; dislocations take the shortest lattice translation vector along the close-packed direction as their Burgers vector. About 0.405 nm is the lattice parameter itself (a translation along <100>), which is unfavorable because the dislocation energy is proportional to b². About 0.351 nm applies the BCC (a/2)<111>, that is, √3a/2. The elastic energy per unit length of a dislocation is about Gb²/2, so dislocations with smaller b are more stable.
